scripts.opening:opening:
[warmly] JAUNT: THE DAUGHTER WHO MADE THINGS. A grey Monday morning, 21 November 1904, at the north end of the Glessner family's world.

Four stops, from the twin houses the Glessners built for their two children, down to the great stone house at Eighteenth Street where the daughter grew up. [short pause] Frances Glessner Lee is 26. She was taught at home, married at 19, [short pause] [intrigued] and she is the last person on this street anyone would expect to change the way murders are investigated. [long pause] [softly] Watch her hands.

[short pause] Start at 1700 Prairie, at the door of the young Lees.
scripts.stop:lees: [warmly] 1700 Prairie, the north half of a pair of twin townhouses. John and Frances Glessner built them for their two children, and the young families moved in in 1902. This one belongs to their daughter Frances and her husband Blewett Lee, a lawyer. She was born in 1878, the youngest child and only daughter, "tutored at home" in the stone house down the street, and she toured Europe at 18. [short pause] On 9 February 1898, at 19, she married Lee in her parents' house; the cook baked the wedding cake. [short pause] [tenderly] Now there is a boy, John, who is six, and a baby girl born last year. [short pause] Watch the front door. Her husband is leaving for his office, [quietly] and she stays on the step. [short pause] Next door lives her brother.
scripts.stop:george: [amused] 1706 Prairie, the other twin, shares a wall with the Lees. Here lives her brother George Glessner, his wife Alice and their four children, Elizabeth, Frances, John and the new baby, Emily, born this year. George takes photographs the way other men breathe; he photographed these very houses going up in 1901, and in 1902 he was made a manager at International Harvester. [short pause] [warmly] His is the kind of life the street understands: a job, a camera, a nursery full of children. [short pause] [thoughtful] His sister's life is supposed to look the same from the sidewalk, and it does. [short pause] [quietly] But her son will say, years later, that what broke her marriage was her "creative urge coupled with high manual dexterity—the desire to make things—which [Lee] did not share." [short pause] [intrigued] Walk south a block to find out where that urge came from.
scripts.stop:mother: [warmly] 1800 Prairie, the house she grew up in, built like a fortress at Eighteenth Street. Her mother, Frances Glessner, is 56, [proudly] and this year she has done something few ladies of Prairie Avenue would do. In 1904 she set up a workbench in the basement and began to make silver with her own hands. She takes lessons from Annibale Fogliata, a master jewelry craftsman of Hull House, and from Madeline Yale Wynne, a Chicago silversmith. [short pause] [delighted] Every piece she makes carries her mark, "a G encircling a honeybee", because she keeps bees as well. She has kept a journal since 1879; [amused] she misses nothing. [short pause] The daughter comes to the door. Inside is a mother who has decided, at 56, to learn a trade.
scripts.stop:court: [softly] The courtyard, the sunny private heart of the fortress. [short pause] The mother shows the daughter what her hands have made. It is easy to see what the daughter sees: a woman of 56 who was given permission by nobody, doing exact, patient, beautiful work at a bench. [short pause] [thoughtful] Frances Glessner Lee is clever, and she is bored, and her marriage is "not a happy one". Her son will say that she had the "creative urge coupled with high manual dexterity" that her husband never shared. [short pause] [intrigued] Everything that happens to her next starts with what she is looking at now: small things, made precisely, by hand, in a house where every detail is a clue. [long pause] She will have one more child. [short pause] Then she will leave, and she will build something nobody on this street could ever have imagined.
scripts.ending:nutshell: [thoughtful] End of the walk. Martha was born in 1906. [short pause] In 1914 the Lees divorced. [short pause] [intrigued] Years later Frances Glessner Lee made the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death: tiny, exact rooms where a death has happened, built at one inch to a foot, [whispers] every clue in place. [short pause] [amused] She wrote to an adviser, "I found myself constantly tempted to add more clues and details…stop me when I go too far." [short pause] [proudly] In 1931 she gave Harvard $250,000 for legal medicine, and in 1943 New Hampshire made her the first woman state police captain in the country. [short pause] Detectives still train on her rooms. [long pause] [warmly] The girl who was tutored at home taught the police how to look.
